Ideally, if it's a vehicle worth saving, you need to take the body off the frame and treat the rust the old fashioned way with a wire brush, metal wool and sand paper, then paint over it.

If it's panel rust, take a wire brush, metal wool and sand paper to it, bondo where necessary. Repaint with a primer coat and there's some videos on Youtube for DIY car painting with spray cans that will at least be as good as MAACO.

There is a product called P.O.R. 15 (Paint Over Rust) I heard people use this and achieve good results.

https://www.por15.com/
I have used this on my 1980 Triumph Spitfire. The floorpans on both sides were getting iffy. P.O.R. 15 is fantastic stuff. I can't recommend it enough.

Remove loose rust with wire brush, remove scale with air chisel, paint with 40% Phosphoric acid with about 0.1% detergent mixed in. Once dry, brush again to remove any white powdery residue, then add your surface coating.

Have done various iron & steel boats this way, including one over 100 yrs old.

Phosphoric acid converts iron oxide into iron phosphate, which is a pretty good surface coating for stopping rust. The detergent breaks down the surface tension a little, helps it penetrate. Phosphoric acid is the main ingredient in most rust-cure products, with the other being citric acid. The main effect of citric acid is to colour the converted rust, in other words it's cosmetic, makes the effect more visual.

Talc has this spot on. That acid should stop the rust, but if you want to preserve the vehicle, get it oil undercoated every year. I used a mineral oil based oil that creeps into spaces for 4 years to stop additional rusting until I could get the body work done.
